Adoption Decision Guide

Source: vignettes/adoption-decision-guide.Rmd
adoption-decision-guide.Rmd

This guide helps decide whether gamlss.longitudinal should be the primary model, a sensitivity model, or not used for a longitudinal analysis. The short version is:

  • use a GEE when the estimand is a marginal mean and the response distribution is routine;
  • use a GLMM when subject-specific latent heterogeneity is the scientific estimand;
  • use gamlss.longitudinal when the applied answer depends on margins, heteroskedasticity, quantiles, tails, asymmetry, or longitudinal dependence.

That framing is deliberately conservative. The package should replace GEE and GLMM workflows where distributional and dependence modelling changes the answer, not by pretending every longitudinal question needs a richer model.

Decision Table

Applied question Default starting point Why
Average marginal treatment effect only GEE The GEE estimand matches the question and is fast.
Subject-specific random-effect interpretation GLMM The random effect is part of the scientific model.
Mean plus calibrated intervals or quantiles gamlss.longitudinal Model mu, sigma, and other margin parameters directly.
Heteroskedastic longitudinal outcome gamlss.longitudinal Put variance drivers in sigma.formula and check interval calibration.
Positive, skewed, count, or tail-sensitive outcome gamlss.longitudinal Choose a GAMLSS family and inspect quantile/tail diagnostics.
Time-varying dependence gamlss.longitudinal Put time or covariates in theta.formula.
Sparse data with weakly identified distributional parameters GEE/GLMM plus sensitivity analysis Richer margins may be unstable.
Regulatory or clinical report requiring a familiar primary model GEE/GLMM plus gamlss.longitudinal sensitivity Keep the primary estimand familiar and report distributional sensitivity.

Translation Table

GEE/GLMM concept GAMLSS-copula concept
Mean formula mu.formula
Working correlation Copula family plus theta.formula
Random intercept as dependence device Copula dependence parameter
Overdispersion or residual scale sigma.formula
Shape, zero inflation, tail behaviour GAMLSS family parameters such as nu or tau
Robust mean-focused diagnostics check_model() marginal, PIT, tail, and dependence decisions
Mean prediction predict(type = "response")
Prediction interval or percentile predict(type = "quantile")
Subject trajectory simulation simulate(type = "copula")

Minimum Evidence For Replacement

A replacement claim needs more than a successful fit. Before making gamlss.longitudinal the primary model, check:

  1. The estimand needs distributional or dependence modelling.
  2. check_model() does not flag unresolved marginal, tail, or dependence problems.
  3. The familiar GEE or GLMM does not answer the same applied question more simply.
  4. Scenario-level benchmarks or sensitivity analyses support the replacement for the relevant estimand.
  5. The report states whether inference is likelihood/Hessian based, delta-method, bootstrap/simulation based, or approximate.

Use vignette("inference-uncertainty", package = "gamlss.longitudinal") as the reporting checklist for that last item.

The benchmark framework is meant to support this evidence:

bench <- run_adoption_benchmarks(
  scenarios = c("gaussian_heteroskedastic", "time_varying_dependence"),
  reps = 100,
  methods = c("rs_separate", "gee", "glmm", "gam"),
  max_elapsed_sec = 60,
  write_results = TRUE
)

write_benchmark_report(bench)

Read the scenario-level sections of the report first. They are restricted to the declared primary metrics for each scenario, which keeps the claim tied to the problem being tested.

When To Use It As The Primary Model

Use gamlss.longitudinal as the primary model when one or more of these are true:

  • clinical or scientific decisions depend on quantiles, tails, or calibrated probabilities;
  • scale, skewness, zero inflation, or tail behaviour changes with covariates;
  • residual dependence remains after a mean-only GEE or random-intercept GLMM;
  • time-varying or covariate-varying dependence is scientifically relevant;
  • simulation, prediction, or subject trajectory generation is part of the deliverable;
  • scenario-level benchmarks show wins or meaningful ties on the relevant estimand.

When To Use It As Sensitivity Analysis

Use it as a sensitivity model when the GEE or GLMM remains the clearest primary analysis, but distributional assumptions still matter. Good sensitivity uses include:

  • checking whether a marginal mean conclusion changes under a richer response family;
  • verifying whether tails or intervals are underfit by a standard model;
  • exploring whether dependence is more structured than a random intercept or exchangeable working correlation;
  • reporting subject-trajectory simulations alongside a familiar primary model.

In this role, the model earns trust by explaining what the simpler model misses, not by replacing it automatically.

When Not To Use It

Do not make gamlss.longitudinal the primary model when:

  • the scientific question is only a marginal mean and a GEE fits cleanly;
  • a random effect is the scientific target rather than a nuisance dependence device;
  • the sample is too small to identify the chosen distributional parameters;
  • the time grid or missingness mechanism requires a model outside the current adjacent-time copula workflow;
  • diagnostics show unresolved marginal, tail, or dependence misfit;
  • benchmark or sensitivity results show no practical gain over the familiar model;
  • stakeholders need a simple estimand and the richer model would obscure the answer.

In those cases, a GEE or GLMM may be the better primary analysis. The GAMLSS-copula model can still be valuable as a transparent sensitivity check.

Suggested Reporting Language

Use specific language:

  • “We used a GAMLSS-copula model as the primary model because the estimand included calibrated upper-tail probabilities.”
  • “The GEE was retained as the primary mean model; the GAMLSS-copula analysis was used as a distributional sensitivity analysis.”
  • “The GAMLSS-copula model improved interval calibration in the scenario-level benchmark, but the GEE remained faster and comparable for the marginal mean.”
  • “We did not use the GAMLSS-copula model as primary because diagnostics showed unresolved tail misfit.”

Avoid broad language:

  • “GAMLSS-copula models replace GEEs.”
  • “The benchmark proves this package always beats GLMMs.”
  • “A more flexible distribution is automatically better.”

The adoption case is strongest when it is narrow, diagnostic-driven, and tied to the estimand.
